## Leviticus 12 – Research Notes

### v. 1–2 (unclean seven days, "as during her menstruation")
- **Ellicott:** He says the phrase is better read as "brings forth seed," meaning the woman has given birth. He also notes that the laws on impurity begin, fittingly, where life begins. Rather, if a woman bringeth forth seed, that is, is delivered of a child. Thus the regulations about impurity naturally begin with the beginning of life. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-12.html
- **Gill:** The seven days match her monthly period. Gill calls the period "an infirmity," a time when she was kept apart from other people. the same number of days, even seven, she was unclean on account of childbirth, as she was for her monthly courses, called here an infirmity or sickness, incident to all females when grown up, at which time they were separate from all persons https://studylight.org/commentaries/geb/leviticus-12.html
- **Matthew Henry:** In the first stage she was strictly separated, and those who cared for her also became unclean. Henry gives this as one reason boys waited until the eighth day to be circumcised. those that necessarily attended her were ceremonially unclean, which was one reason why the males were not circumcised till the eighth day, because they participated in the mother's pollution during the days of her separation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_012.cfm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** He says the key is original sin. The rite was a reminder that every birth brings another sinner into the world. Guzik also says the laws do not look down on childbearing, since Scripture commands and blesses it (Gen 1:28; Ps 127:3; Ps 128:3). He quotes G. Campbell Morgan, who reads Psalm 51:5 as stating "a racial fact" and not casting blame on David's mother. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **Constable:** "Unclean" does not mean "sinful." Childbearing was one of the things that made a person ritually unclean without being morally wrong. ceremonial defilement (ritual uncleanness) did not necessarily mean that the defiled person had sinned. Some practices that resulted in ceremonial uncleanness were not morally wrong in themselves, such as childbearing. Therefore we must not think "sinful" whenever we read "unclean." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-6.html
- **Precept Austin (Reformation Study Bible note and others):** The bleeding after birth is what made the mother unclean. Loss of blood could lead to death, thus illustrating the equation of uncleanness with death. The chapter does not teach that sex, pregnancy or babies are impure. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60790/

### v. 3 (circumcision on the eighth day)
- **Guzik:** Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Gen 17:11–12). It cut away the flesh, which made it a fitting sign for people who must not trust in the flesh. Because it involved the organ of procreation, it also recalled the promised seed of Abraham, who would ultimately bring the Messiah. Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 2:21). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **Precept Austin:** This is the only mention of circumcision in Leviticus, and it comes up almost in passing, because the chapter's focus is the mother. One cited view says the rite also carried an idea of cleansing, as well as entry into the covenant people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60790/
- **Constable:** He disagrees with that view. The Law did not regard a newborn child as unclean, and circumcision was not a purification rite for the child. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-6.html
- **Where traditions differ (infant baptism):** Guzik (Calvary Chapel, on the Pentecostal/charismatic list) links circumcision to Colossians 2:11–12. He then argues against infant baptism: One is not genetically born into the New Covenant; one is born again into it by God's grace through faith. It is wrong and harmful to make the analogy, "babies were circumcised, so babies should be baptized." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-12.cfm
  - *The opposing view (Reformed and Lutheran infant baptism) did not come up on this chapter.* The only hint is the Expositor's Bible, quoted on StudyLight's Spanish page. It speaks of Christ receiving little ones into covenant from infancy through a "circumcision made without hands." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-4.html

### v. 4 (thirty-three more days; must not touch anything holy or enter the sanctuary)
- **Guzik:** The total is 40 days. He calls it an ancient form of maternity leave: being unclean freed her from social duties and gave her time to rest and bond with the baby. Because life is in the blood (Lev 17:11), losing blood called for purification. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **Matthew Henry:** In this second stage she was barred only from the sanctuary and from holy food such as the Passover and peace offerings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_012.cfm
- **Gill:** She was partly freed after seven days, but her blood went on being purified until it was complete at forty days. https://studylight.org/commentaries/geb/leviticus-12.html
- **Constable (quoting another writer):** "Impurity" here means being shut out of worship. It is not a vague taboo. Impurity is not defined in terms of a vague notion of taboo but in terms of acceptance or restriction from worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-8.html

### v. 5 (a daughter: double the time, 14 + 66 days)
The longer time for a daughter is the most debated point in the chapter. The explanations people give:
- **The daughter will one day bear sinners herself (Guzik):** The longer period is not a penalty. It reflects that a daughter is a sinner who will bring more sinners into the world. Some also suggest that girls are smaller at birth, or that the extra time made families bond with a daughter when sons were valued more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **We can't know (Matthew Henry):** I can assign no reason but the will of the Law-maker; in Christ Jesus no difference is made of male and female https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_012.cfm
- **The boy's circumcision bears part of the cleansing (Gill and the Pulpit Commentary):** Gill reports a Jewish view that a girl's birth involves a heavier flow. He prefers the view that a circumcised boy, through his own shed blood, carries part of the purification. He also cites Hippocrates for a longer flow after a girl's birth, but says the rule rests mainly on the Lawgiver's will. https://studylight.org/commentaries/geb/leviticus-12.html The Pulpit Commentary similarly says the impurity attached to both mother and child, and circumcision made the boy clean. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-4.html
- **No physical reason (Clarke):** He finds no physical or political explanation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-6.html
- **A reminder of Eve's curse; the shorter time hints at a male Deliverer (Coffman):** He notes that some scholars point to how ancient cultures valued girls less. He insists no sin attaches to either child. He reads the 80 days as a reminder of the penalty on Eve, and the shorter time for a boy as pointing to a coming male Deliverer. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/leviticus-12.html
- **Jewish view of holiness (GotQuestions):** It reports the Jewish tradition that the time doubles because both mother and daughter are being purified. It rejects the "bonding" and "hoped-for Messiah" theories as not found in the text. Its own conclusion is something spiritual, possibly a reminder of Eve's sin. https://www.gotquestions.org/unclean-daughter-longer-son.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible note):** The boy's circumcision had to happen on day eight, so the mother's impurity could not run past seven days. Bleeding after birth is heavier than a normal period, so fourteen days may have been the natural length. On this view, the boy's period was shortened rather than the girl's lengthened. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Lev&chapter=12

### v. 6 (burnt offering of a year-old lamb; bird for a sin offering)
- **Ellicott:** The offerings came on day 41 or day 81. The purification was for the mother, not the baby, who was not unclean. He reports ancient guesses about the meaning. The burnt offering expressed thanks, or confessed impatient thoughts during pregnancy. The sin offering covered rash words spoken in labour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/12-6.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary (via Bible Hub):** The burnt offering costs more than the sin offering. The sin offering was not for any personal sin, only for human sin shown indirectly in her bodily condition (Keil). Unusually, the burnt offering comes first here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/12-6.htm
- **Matthew Poole:** The sin offering was either for her ritual uncleanness or for sins she could be presumed to have committed while bearing the child. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/12-6.htm
- **Guzik:** The lamb marked the child's dedication to God. The bird was a sin offering for atonement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/

### v. 7 (atonement; "she shall be cleansed")
- **Ellicott:** Of the two offerings, the stress falls on the sin offering, because her purification and atonement depended on it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-12.html
- **Guzik:** The sacrifice was the same whether she had a boy or a girl. He quotes Morgan: if people are born in sin, God has still made a way back into fellowship with him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **NET Bible note:** It reads the sin offering as cleaning impurity out of the tabernacle. In this case, the woman has not "sinned" morally by having a child. The result is "she will be clean," not "she will be forgiven" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Lev&chapter=12
- **Constable:** Her presence in the camp had affected the altar even though she stayed away from it, which is why a purification offering was needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-6.html

### v. 8 (two birds for a woman who cannot afford a lamb)
- **Gill:** The poor mother's atonement counted just as fully as if she had brought a lamb. Mary brought this offering (Luke 2:24), which shows the family was poor and that both mother and child kept the law. https://studylight.org/commentaries/geb/leviticus-12.html
- **Matthew Henry:** The sin offering was the same for rich and poor. The difference came only in the offering of thanks. Christ was "made under the law" early in life to redeem those under it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_012.cfm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/12-8.html
- **Guzik:** Because Mary brought birds, he says the wise men's costly gifts had not yet arrived. He quotes F. B. Meyer on how far Christ humbled himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
- **Bible Hub summary:** No one is shut out from God's presence because of poverty. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/12.htm

### Where traditions differ: Mary's purification (vv. 6–8 and Luke 2)
- **Catholic:** The Purification of the Blessed Virgin is kept on 2 February, under the name Candlemas. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Mary kept this law forty days after Christ's birth. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03245b.htm A Catholic Answers article cites Protestant scholar L. Michael Morales to argue that Leviticus 12 deals with temporary ritual impurity, not sinfulness. So Mary's two pigeons were not for repairing a sinful relationship with God. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/breaking-immaculate-mary-made-a-sin-offering
- **Orthodox:** The OCA keeps the feast as the "Meeting of the Lord," and its evening readings include the purification law of Leviticus. https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-church-year/meeting-of-the-lord The OCA's life of the feast says Mary had no need of purification, because she had given birth to the source of purity, but kept the law out of humility. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/02/02/100407-the-meeting-of-our-lord-and-savior-jesus-christ-in-the-temple The Orthodox rite of "churching" around the fortieth day copies this Old Testament practice. The mother returns to the Divine Liturgy after her absence during her confinement after the birth. https://www.oca.org/orthodoxy/the-orthodox-faith/worship/the-sacraments/chrismation
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** It argues that medieval devotion to Mary moved her "purification" to centre stage. As a result, the "Presentation of the Lord" became detached from the text, when the early church had treated Jesus as the key figure in Luke 2. https://www.1517.org/articles/ever-heard-of-candlemas
- **Anglican:** An older encyclopedia describes the "churching of women" as a thanksgiving service after childbirth. It was used in the Church of England and the Episcopal Church (as well as the Greek and Roman churches), derived from the rite of purification enjoined in the twelfth chapter of Leviticus https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/c/churching-of-women.html
- **Protestant commentators on whether Mary sinned:** Matthew Henry says Christ was not conceived in sin as others are, yet Mary still completed the purification. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_012.cfm Guzik says Mary was not bringing a sinner into the world, but Jesus identified with sinful humanity even as an infant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-12/
